questions.prompt: By default, what user does a container's process run as, and why is that a concern?

options.text: A random user; it is never a concern
root (unless a USER is set); a compromise then gives an attacker root inside the container
nobody; it is fully safe
The host's logged-in user

questions.explanation: Unless the image sets a USER, the process runs as root. Running unprivileged limits what an attacker can do if the app is compromised.

questions.prompt: Why can't you hide a secret by COPYing it into an image and deleting it in a later instruction?

options.text: Because Docker encrypts all layers
Because the secret is stored in the layer created by the COPY, and later layers do not erase earlier ones
Because deletes are not allowed in Dockerfiles
It actually does hide the secret safely

questions.explanation: Each instruction adds a layer; the secret remains in the earlier layer and can be extracted, even if a later instruction appears to remove the file.

questions.prompt: How do you provide a secret during a build without baking it into the image?

options.text: Pass it with ARG
Use a BuildKit build secret: RUN --mount=type=secret with docker build --secret
Set it as an ENV
COPY it in and delete it

questions.explanation: A BuildKit build secret is mounted only for that RUN and never written to a layer, unlike ARG or ENV which persist in the image.

questions.prompt: Docker's built-in tool for scanning images for known vulnerabilities is Docker ______. (one word)
questions.explanation: docker scout cves <image> lists known CVEs in an image's packages; scanning belongs in CI so vulnerable images are caught early.

questions.prompt: Which practices apply least privilege to a container? Select all that apply.

options.text: Run with --read-only and mount a small tmpfs for paths that need writes
Use --cap-drop ALL and add back only the capabilities needed
Add --security-opt no-new-privileges
Run with --privileged to be safe

questions.explanation: Read-only filesystems, dropped capabilities, and no-new-privileges all reduce privilege. --privileged does the opposite, removing most isolation.

questions.prompt: Which base-image habit best reduces the number of vulnerabilities you ship?

options.text: Use the largest possible base image
Prefer minimal, trusted, pinned base images and rebuild regularly to pick up patches
Always use :latest and never rebuild
Avoid official images

questions.explanation: Minimal images have a smaller attack surface, trusted/pinned images are predictable, and regular rebuilds pull in upstream security patches.
